# forgesworn/anvil

> Forge-hardened release tool for JS/TS libraries. Multi-runner
> reproducible-build attestation, OIDC trusted publishing, SLSA
> provenance, pre-publish secret scan, exports-map check, frozen-vector
> gate, runtime-only npm audit, action-pin auditing. Pure bash, ~1600
> lines, auditable in thirty minutes.
>
> Not to be confused with Foundry's `anvil` (Ethereum dev node) or
> anvil.works (low-code app platform). This is a GitHub Action for
> npm release pipelines.

## What this is

A GitHub Action (reusable workflow + composite fallback) that publishes
npm packages with hard pre-publish gates. Zero dependencies, pure bash,
auditable in thirty minutes.

The flagship feature: two parallel CI builds on independent runners must
produce byte-identical tarballs, or the release is blocked. No other
JS release tool offers this today.

## Who it's for

Any JavaScript/TypeScript library author who publishes to npm and wants
a release pipeline with fewer moving parts than the library it ships.
Especially useful for libraries where a compromised publish would matter
-- authentication, payments, cryptography, infrastructure -- but the
gates are valuable for any package.

## How to use it

Five-line caller workflow in your library's `.github/workflows/release.yml`:

```yaml
name: release
on:
  release:
    types: [published]
permissions:
  contents: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  release:
    uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/release.yml@v0
    with:
      vector-test-command: npm run test:vectors
```

Configure npm trusted publishing on npmjs.com for YOUR repo and YOUR
caller workflow file (not forgesworn/anvil). Bump package.json,
tag, push, create a GitHub Release. The workflow handles everything
else.

## Auto-release (zero-dep semantic-release replacement)

For fully automatic releases from conventional commits on main, add
an auto-release.yml workflow. It parses commits since the last tag,
bumps package.json, updates CHANGELOG.md, tags, pushes, and fires
release.yml via workflow_dispatch.

Auto mode is a two-file setup. Your release.yml must declare a
workflow_dispatch trigger with a tag input:

```yaml
name: release
on:
  release:
    types: [published]       # manual flow
  workflow_dispatch:         # auto flow dispatches here
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: Release tag to publish
        type: string
        required: true
permissions:
  contents: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  release:
    uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/release.yml@v0
    with:
      tag: ${{ inputs.tag || '' }}
```

Then add the auto-release caller:

```yaml
name: auto-release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: write
  actions: write            # required to dispatch release.yml
jobs:
  auto-release:
    uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/auto-release.yml@v0
```

No PAT needed (workflow_dispatch is an exception to GitHub's anti-
recursion rule). Trusted-publisher config on npmjs.com continues to
point at release.yml — the workflow_dispatch bridge preserves
release.yml as the OIDC entry-point.

All release-time inputs (vector-test-command, reproducibility-mode,
audit-level, etc.) live on release.yml. auto-release.yml accepts
only: release-branch, release-workflow, package-json, changelog-file,
dry-run.

## Architecture

The reusable workflow runs as a four-job DAG:

- **build-a**: all gates (tag match, tests, vectors, audit, exports,
  secrets, action pins) then npm pack with normalised mtimes
- **build-b**: parallel build + pack on a second runner
- **reproduce**: compare sha256s; strict mode blocks on mismatch
- **publish**: upload the canonical tarball to npm, update the GitHub
  Release body with an artefact-integrity block, upload the tarball as
  a release asset

## Step scripts

All in `steps/`, all bash, all sourcing `lib.sh` for shared helpers:

| Script | Purpose |
|---|---|
| verify-tag.sh | Git tag matches package.json version |
| run-tests.sh | Full test suite |
| verify-vectors.sh | Frozen-vector gate |
| verify-audit.sh | npm audit --omit=dev |
| verify-exports.sh | Every exports subpath exists on disk |
| verify-secrets.sh | Secret scan over pack set |
| verify-action-pins.sh | Warn/fail on unpinned uses: in workflows |
| normalise-mtimes.sh | Touch all files to SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH |
| record-tarball.sh | npm pack, hash, write tarball.meta |
| compare-tarball-meta.sh | Reproducibility gate (compare two metas) |
| publish-npm.sh | Publish the exact recorded tarball via OIDC |
| publish-jsr.sh | JSR publish if jsr.json exists |
| update-release.sh | CHANGELOG extraction, integrity block, asset upload |
| changelog-extract.sh | Parse CHANGELOG.md for the version section |
| lib.sh | Shared helpers (header, log, warn, die, require_cmds) |

## Exports-map check (verify-exports.sh)

Catches the "I deleted src/foo.ts but forgot to update exports" class of
bug before it ships a broken import to downstream consumers. Neither
`publint` nor `arethetypeswrong` perform this file-existence check.

### What it validates

**Modern exports field:** Uses jq to walk the entire `.exports` tree in
`package.json`, including all conditional keys (`import`, `require`,
`types`, `node`, `browser`, `default`), nested conditionals, and string
shorthand. Every leaf string starting with `./` is treated as a path
that must exist on disk.

**Legacy entry points:** Also checks top-level `main`, `module`,
`types`, `typings`, and `bin` (both string and object forms). These are
the pre-exports world but still shipped to consumers. Paths without a
`./` prefix are normalised automatically.

Duplicate paths (e.g. when `default` repeats an `import` target) are
deduplicated so each file is checked exactly once.

### Configuration

No special configuration required. The check runs automatically as part
of the build-a job. The only relevant input is `package-json` (defaults
to `package.json`) which controls the path to the manifest file.

### How it enforces the gate

- If any exported path does not exist on disk, the step exits with
  status 1 and the release is blocked.
- Output on failure: `warning: missing: ./dist/missing.js` for each
  missing path, then `error: N exports targets missing on disk —
  refusing to publish`.
- Output on success: `ok  ./dist/index.js` for each path, then
  `ok: all N export targets exist`.
- If no exports or legacy entry points are declared, the check warns
  and passes (exit 0).

### Example package.json triggering the check

```json
{
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "import": "./dist/index.mjs",
      "require": "./dist/index.cjs",
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts"
    },
    "./utils": {
      "import": "./dist/utils.mjs",
      "require": "./dist/utils.cjs"
    }
  },
  "main": "./dist/index.cjs",
  "types": "./dist/index.d.ts"
}
```

All six paths (four from exports, two from legacy main/types) must exist
after the build step. If `./dist/utils.mjs` is missing, the release is
blocked.

## Runtime-only npm audit (verify-audit.sh)

Runs `npm audit --omit=dev` so that devDependency advisories do not
block releases, but any advisory in the runtime dependency tree does.
This is the opposite of tools like semantic-release, which audit
everything and drown you in devDep noise that has zero impact on
consumers of your published package.

### How it works

The script runs a single command:

```sh
npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=$level
```

The `--omit=dev` flag tells npm to evaluate only production dependencies
(those in `dependencies`, not `devDependencies`). If npm finds any
advisory at or above the configured severity level, it exits non-zero
and the release is blocked.

### Configuration

The `audit-level` input (default: `low`) controls the severity
threshold. Valid values are `low`, `moderate`, `high`, and `critical`.
For security-sensitive libraries (cryptography, authentication,
payments), the default of `low` is intentional: even low-severity
runtime advisories are worth investigating before publishing.

```yaml
uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/release.yml@v0
with:
  audit-level: moderate   # only block on moderate or above
```

### What it checks and what it ignores

- **Checked**: all packages in `dependencies` (the runtime tree that
  ships to consumers)
- **Ignored**: all packages in `devDependencies` (build tools, test
  frameworks, linters -- these never reach consumers)

No additional configuration in `package.json` is required. The check
runs automatically as part of the build-a job.

## Tarball hash stamping (record-tarball.sh + update-release.sh)

After all pre-publish gates pass and the package is published to npm,
anvil stamps the registry tarball's cryptographic hashes into the GitHub
Release body and uploads the tarball as a release asset. This gives
consumers two independent sources for the bytes (npm registry + GitHub
Releases) and a way to verify they match.

### How it works (two-step process)

**Step 1 -- record-tarball.sh** (runs in the build job):

1. Derives `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` from the git commit timestamp
2. Normalises all file mtimes to that epoch (for reproducibility)
3. Runs `npm pack --json` to produce the canonical tarball
4. Computes sha256 via `shasum -a 256`
5. Extracts the npm integrity value (sha512) from `npm pack --json`
6. Writes all metadata to `tarball.meta` (key=value format):
   `filename`, `size`, `sha256`, `integrity`

**Step 2 -- update-release.sh** (runs in the publish job):

1. Extracts the changelog section for this version
2. Reads `tarball.meta` and appends an "Artefact integrity" block:

```
---

## Artefact integrity

file:      my-package-1.2.0.tgz
size:      12345 bytes
sha256:    abc123...
sha512-base64...

Verify against the registry tarball:

curl -sLO https://registry.npmjs.org/my-package/-/my-package-1.2.0.tgz
shasum -a 256 my-package-1.2.0.tgz
```

3. If the reproducible-build gate confirmed two independent builds
   matched, a "Reproducible build" badge is added above the block
4. Uploads the tarball as a GitHub Release asset via `gh release upload`

### Configuration

No configuration required. The stamping runs automatically whenever the
publish job succeeds. The integrity block appears in the GitHub Release
body and the tarball appears as a downloadable release asset.

### What consumers can verify

A consumer can download the tarball from the npm registry and compare
its sha256 against the value stamped in the GitHub Release body. If the
hashes match, the bytes on npm are the same bytes CI built. If the
reproducible-build badge is present, those bytes were also confirmed
identical across two independent CI runners.

## Action-pin auditing (verify-action-pins.sh)

Walks `.github/workflows/*.yml` in the consumer's repository and flags
every `uses: owner/repo@ref` reference whose ref is not a 40-character
hex SHA. This catches the supply-chain risk where a tag-pinned action
(`@v4`) can be silently re-pointed at malicious code -- the same vector
that hit `tj-actions/changed-files` in March 2025.

### How it works

For each workflow file, the script extracts every `uses:` line and
checks whether the `@ref` portion is a full 40-character commit SHA.
References that use tags (`@v4`), branches (`@main`), or short SHAs are
flagged as unpinned.

Special cases:
- **Local actions** (`./ paths`): skipped (resolved from the same repo)
- **forgesworn/anvil**: self-exempt to avoid circular failure, but warns
  if the consumer has not SHA-pinned anvil itself
- **Docker references**: checks for `sha256:` digest pinning

### Configuration

The `strict-action-pins` input (default: `true`) controls whether
unpinned references block the release or only warn:

```yaml
uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/release.yml@v0
with:
  strict-action-pins: true    # fail on unpinned refs (default)
  strict-action-pins: false   # warn only, do not block
```

### Output

- Warning per unpinned ref: `unpinned action: .github/workflows/ci.yml:12  actions/setup-node@v4`
- In strict mode: `error: N unpinned action reference(s) found`
  and exit 1 (release blocked)
- In warn mode: logs the count and suggests SHA pins, but exits 0

## Key inputs (reusable workflow)

| Input | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| node-version | 24.11.0 | Node version (must ship npm >= 11.5.x for OIDC; 22 LTS ships 10.9.x which is too old) |
| registry-url | https://registry.npmjs.org | npm registry URL |
| test-command | npm test | Full test suite command |
| vector-test-command | (empty) | Frozen-vector gate command (skip if empty) |
| changelog-file | CHANGELOG.md | Path to changelog |
| package-json | package.json | Path to package.json |
| audit-level | low | npm audit threshold (low/moderate/high/critical) |
| version-strategy | manual | manual: you bump and tag; verify: also checks conventional commits match your bump |
| reproducibility-mode | strict | strict: block on mismatch; warn: log only; off: skip build-b and reproduce jobs entirely |
| strict-action-pins | true | Fail on unpinned `uses:` refs in consumer workflows |
| tag | (empty) | Explicit release tag (e.g. `v1.2.3`). Set by `auto-release.yml`'s workflow_dispatch bridge via `${{ inputs.tag || '' }}`. Empty defaults to `github.event.release.tag_name` for the legacy release-event trigger path. |
| dry-run | false | Skip real publish |
| debug | false | Diagnostic logging for OIDC issues |

The composite action (`uses: forgesworn/anvil@v0`) accepts the same
inputs *except* `reproducibility-mode` (the composite cannot run the
two-build DAG — use the reusable workflow for reproducible-build
verification).

Composite action callers must add `actions/checkout` before the step
(the reusable workflow handles checkout internally):

```yaml
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: forgesworn/anvil@v0
        with:
          vector-test-command: npm run test:vectors
```

For JSR dual-publish via the reusable workflow, pass the JSR token as
a secret:

```yaml
jobs:
  release:
    uses: forgesworn/anvil/.github/workflows/release.yml@v0
    secrets:
      JSR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.JSR_TOKEN }}
```
